document.title: Afghanistan and Sectarian Violence Contribute to a Souring of Pakistan's Relations with Iran (Islama 02001)
document.publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), Pakistan: "The Taliban's Godfather"?
document.note: [Confidential] Discusses how Pakistan's Taliban support harms ties with Iran. The U.S. should steer clear of Pakistan-Iran disputes. Pakistan denies being the Taliban's godfather, though officials privately acknowledge close links and supplying foodstuffs and fuel.

events.description: Iranian revolution establishes Shia regime, souring relations with Pakistan.
Soviet forces withdraw from Afghanistan.
Communist regime in Kabul falls, opening competition for influence between Pakistan and Iran.
Taliban seize Herat, fueling Iranian concerns.
Kabul falls to the Taliban.
Iranian diplomat gunned down in Lahore.
Bomb blast in Lahore killed 26 including an SSP leader; top SSP leader seriously wounded.
Sahabzada Yaqub Khan visits Tehran to ease Iranian doubts about Pakistani policy and the Taliban.
Iranian cultural attache assassinated in Multan with several Pakistanis.
US Embassy Islamabad sends cable on souring Pakistan-Iran relations.
Meeting with CINCCENT General Peay, in which it was stated that Iran has 13-14 cultural centers in Pakistan.
Indian FM Gujral made a highly publicized visit to Tehran.
US Embassy Islamabad cables assessment of souring Pakistan-Iran relations over Afghanistan and sectarian violence, and recommends US policy.
Soviet forces withdrew from Afghanistan, setting the stage for Pakistani-Iranian competition for influence.
The communist regime in Kabul fell.
Rise of the Taliban in southwestern Afghanistan in late 1994/early 1995.
The Taliban seized Herat, fueling Iranian fears of being ousted from Afghanistan.
Kabul fell to the Taliban.
Caretaker FM Sahabzada Yaqub Khan visited Tehran to dispel Iranian doubts about Pakistan and the Taliban.
Newly independent Central Asian states emerged from the Soviet Union, and Pakistan and Iran began competing for influence there.
Bomb blast in Lahore killed 26 people, including a leader of the SSP; the top SSP leader was seriously wounded.
The Iranian cultural attache was assassinated in Multan along with several Pakistanis.
An Iranian diplomat was gunned down in Lahore.
Meeting with CINCCENT General Peay, where it was said Iran has 13-14 cultural centers in Pakistan.
A Unocal representative told the Embassy political officer that the pipeline environment was so politically charged that every business decision must be reviewed for international repercussions.
Indian Foreign Minister Gujral made a highly publicized visit to Tehran.
US Embassy Islamabad sent cable 02001 on Pakistan-Iran relations, coordinated with consulates in Karachi, Lahore and Peshawar, advising the U.S. to steer clear of Pak-Iran problems.
Establishment of the Shia regime in Iran following the revolution, beginning a bumpy phase in Pakistan-Iran relations.
Conversation between a Pakistani contact and the U.S. Embassy political officer on Pakistani discomfort with the Shia clerical regime in Iran.
US Embassy Islamabad cable to the State Department analyzing the souring of Pakistan-Iran relations over Afghanistan and sectarian violence.

key_claims: Pakistan-Iran relations soured largely due to Iranian concern over the Sunni Taliban in Afghanistan.
Taliban seizure of Herat in September 1995 deepened Iranian fears and triggered harsh Iranian media attacks on Pakistan as the Taliban's 'puppetmaster'.
Pakistan publicly denies being the Taliban's godfather but privately acknowledges close links and fuel and food supplies.
Iran is building an anti-Taliban alliance and tensions are expected to grow if the Taliban advance on Mazar-i-Sharif.
Pakistan and Iran compete over Central Asian pipeline routes, with Pakistan favoring routes via Afghanistan.
Sectarian violence in Punjab involving SSP and Shia parties adds tension, though there is little concrete evidence linking Iran to it.
The Taliban will likely continue moving north to seize the rest of Afghanistan, though success is not a foregone conclusion.
The proxy war in Afghanistan will keep Pakistan-Iran tensions simmering.
Fresh sectarian attacks in Pakistan could further sour Pakistan-Iran relations.
Pakistanis feel squeezed on two sides by India and Iran over Afghanistan.
No acute Pakistan-Iran crisis is foreseen because of countervailing economic and regional pressures.
The US should avoid involvement in Pak-Iran issues and support UN efforts for a broad-based Afghan government.
